questions.question: What is the AI-gateway pattern for secrets management in 2026?
options: Embed API keys directly in each service's environment variables at deploy time
Apps talk to a gateway which pulls credentials from vault at runtime — rotate in vault and all apps pick up in minutes
Use short-lived tokens generated per-request by each service independently
Store encrypted secrets in the database and decrypt at application startup
questions.explanation: The 2026 pattern: apps route to a gateway, the gateway pulls credentials from HashiCorp Vault / AWS Secrets Manager / Azure Key Vault at runtime. Rotating credentials in vault propagates to all apps immediately with no redeploys and no Slack threads about the new key.

questions.question: What maximum rotation period does the lesson prescribe for API keys and credentials?
options: 7 days
30 days
90 days
180 days
questions.explanation: The lesson prescribes rotation policy of 90 days or less. Longer rotation windows increase the blast radius if a credential is compromised — attackers have more time with valid credentials.

questions.question: What was the 2026 Vercel supply-chain incident cited in the lesson?
options: Vercel's CDN was hijacked to serve malicious JavaScript to all customers
Compromised CI/CD credentials exfiltrated environment variables across thousands of customer deployments
A rogue Vercel employee leaked source code from private repositories
Vercel's DNS provider was compromised, redirecting customer domains to phishing sites
questions.explanation: The 2026 incident: a supply-chain attack via compromised CI/CD credentials resulted in environment variables being exfiltrated across thousands of Vercel customer deployments. This is the canonical example for why CI/CD must use OIDC-based short-lived tokens rather than static secrets.

questions.question: What is consistent tokenization (the Mesh approach) for PII scrubbing, and why does it matter?
options: Replace every PII value with a random UUID that changes per request, ensuring no two requests share a token
Map each unique PII value to a stable placeholder so the LLM preserves code and relationship semantics across a conversation
Tokenize PII values using the same tokenizer as the LLM to preserve token count
Store PII tokens in the KV cache so they can be retrieved if the conversation resumes
questions.explanation: Consistent tokenization maps each unique sensitive value to the same stable placeholder across the conversation. 'Alice' always becomes '[PERSON_1]', not a random ID each time. This lets the LLM understand that [PERSON_1] and [PERSON_1] are the same entity while preventing PII leakage.

questions.question: Which three secret-scanning tools does the lesson recommend for running on every commit?
options: SonarQube, Semgrep, and Snyk
TruffleHog, GitGuardian, and Gitleaks
Bandit, Safety, and pip-audit
Checkov, tfsec, and Trivy
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends TruffleHog (regex + entropy analysis on commits), GitGuardian (commercial, high accuracy), and Gitleaks (open-source, runs in CI). All three run on every commit to catch accidental credential exposure before it reaches the remote.

questions.question: What network egress policy should LLM services enforce to prevent data exfiltration?
options: Allow all outbound traffic within the VPC; block only external internet access
Place LLM services in a dedicated VPC subnet whitelisting only known model provider endpoints; block all other outbound
Use a web proxy that logs all outbound requests for audit purposes
Rely on the cloud provider's default VPC security groups
questions.explanation: LLM services should sit in a dedicated VPC/VNet subnet with egress whitelisted only to specific endpoints: api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com, vector DB endpoints, vault endpoints. Everything else is dropped. This prevents compromised containers from exfiltrating data to arbitrary destinations.
